query: What is the book Dune?
note: Single FindByTitle. Simplest possible book lookup — one node, exact title, no ambiguity.

query: Find the book with ISBN 9780385333481.
note: Single FindByISBN13. Most precise retrieval — ISBN is unambiguous, zero inference needed.

query: Recommend me a mystery book.
note: SUBJECT-ANCHORED RECOMMEND (note rewritten 2026-08-21). "Mystery" is a word the catalog's text contains, so it is keywords=["mystery"] on Retrieve_by_Lexical_Traits, not a genre — genre is only fiction/non-fiction. That retrieval is the anchor Analyze_Similar_Books picks from. The failure to catch is Analyze_Similar_Books alone with semantic_input="mystery": it has no anchor to depend on, and it sends a lexical subject through a similarity search that another node answers exactly.

query: Who is the developer of this app?
note: Single DeveloperInfo. About-me query for the builder of the project.

query: Tell me about this project.
note: Single ProjectInfo. Broad info request; fields=[ALL] is the right response.

query: I want to read something spooky.
note: Single Recommend with mood-based semantic input. No genre enum, LLM must infer horror/thriller theme.

query: Find Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone by J.K. Rowling.
note: Title plus author (design-intent expectation, updated 2026-07-28 when FindByTitle lost its authors hint field). Two retrieval dimensions on the same book, so the pairing is expressed by composition: Retrieve_by_Title + Retrieve_by_Author + Combine_Intersect. The failures to catch are dropping the author entirely (one title node) and pooling the two retrievals without the intersect, which answers 'Harry Potter OR anything by Rowling'.

query: Show me children's books.
note: AUDIENCE-ONLY RETRIEVAL (re-baselined 2026-08-21). One Retrieve_by_Lexical_Traits with audience=children and no keyword at all — a shelf-only search is complete without a subject. The old note claimed is_children=True on the numeric filter; that was never going to work, because books.is_children is NULL on all 5,197 rows and the bound matches nothing. Audience is answered against books.genre (447 books) and that is why this node owns it. The failure to catch is a Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits with is_children set, which returns zero books and reads as an empty catalog.

query: This app is amazing, keep up the great work!
note: Single Feedback with no contact info. Tests that positive small-talk-style text routes to Provide_Feedback, not small_talk.

query: How many tokens have I used so far?
note: Single UserInfo with field=[token_usage]. Simple account-info retrieval.

query: Recommend me a sci-fi novel with at least 4 stars.
note: Single Recommend with semantic input and a min_rating filter. One step up from pure semantic.

query: Find books with fewer than 200 pages.
note: BOUNDS AS THE SUBJECT (re-baselined 2026-08-20, when Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits landed; note updated 2026-08-24). Page count is the whole request — one condition, so there is nothing to intersect it with and no combine node belongs here. Contrast case 77, the same bound with a subject beside it, which takes three nodes. Previously expected no nodes, on the since-reversed premise that a measurable limit can never be what a search is about.

query: What non-fiction books about history do you have?
note: Single FindByTraits with genre=non-fiction and keywords=[history]. Two filters, still one node.

query: Who is the developer and what is their LinkedIn profile?
note: Single DeveloperInfo with field=[name, linkedin_url]. Multi-field but still one retrieval node.

query: Show me the highest rated books you have.
note: SUPERLATIVE AS A BOUND (re-baselined 2026-08-20). 'Highest rated' becomes a tighter rating floor (min_rating 4.3), not a sort: deferred queries carry no ORDER BY, and materialize_stmt already ranks by rating. Previously expected Retrieve_Popular, a node that only ever existed in playground/app_mock/. The failure to catch is an empty filter — the parse must infer a number from a word with no figure in the query.

query: I loved Dune, what should I read next?
note: FindByTitle then Recommend. Classic two-step: resolve the anchor book, then recommend based on it.

query: Compare 1984 and Brave New World.
note: Two FindByTitle then Compare. Minimal three-node chain — no criteria, just a general compare.

query: What books are similar to ISBN 9780385333481?
note: FindByISBN13 then Recommend. Same chain as title-based recommendation but anchored on ISBN.

query: Find fantasy books published between 2010 and 2020 sorted by rating.
note: Single FindByTraits with keyword, year range, and sort. Multiple filters on one node; tests compound filter composition.

query: Recommend me something like Harry Potter but for adults.
note: FindByTitle then Recommend with semantic modifier (adult-oriented). LLM must carry the 'but for adults' into semantic_input.

query: Find me a thriller from the 1990s with more than 300 pages and a rating above 4.
note: Single FindByTraits with keyword + year range + min_pages + min_rating. Four simultaneous filters; tests all numeric constraints together.

query: Recommend me books like The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy sorted by rating.
note: FindByTitle then Recommend with sort_by=rating. Two-node chain where the filter travels to the recommend step.

query: Compare the themes of Pride and Prejudice and Jane Eyre.
note: Two FindByTitle then Compare with comparison_criteria=themes. The planner must extract criteria from the query.

query: What books by Stephen King have over 400 pages?
note: Single FindByTraits with author filter + min_pages. Tests author as a filter field rather than a title-level hint.

query: I want a dark fantasy epic — long, highly rated, published after 2000.
note: Single Recommend with rich semantic_input plus three filters (min_pages implied, min_rating, min_year). No reference book needed.

query: Recommend me something like Dune but shorter and more recent.
note: FindByTitle then Recommend with max_pages and min_year constraints. LLM must translate 'shorter' and 'more recent' into filter values.

query: Find me books about artificial intelligence that are non-fiction and highly rated.
note: SUBJECT + BOUND, INTERSECTED (re-baselined 2026-08-24; previously Retrieve_by_Lexical_Traits + Filter_Retrieval, and Retrieve_Popular before that). The request has a subject (artificial intelligence, non-fiction) AND a rating bound, and since Filter_Retrieval was replaced by Combine_Intersect each gets its own retrieval goal: keywords=["artificial intelligence"] with genre=non-fiction on the lexical node, min_rating on the numeric node, then one intersect over both. The failure to catch is now the opposite of what it used to be: emitting the two retrievals as bare siblings and stopping, which pools them (OR) and answers with more books than either condition alone.

query: Recommend me books like The Hunger Games and Divergent.
note: Two FindByTitle then Recommend with multiple reference_books. Tests that both titles resolve before the recommendation step.

query: What is the GitHub repo for this project?
note: Single ProjectInfo with fields=[project_github_url, project_github_repo_name]. Tests specific project field extraction.

query: Find me a cozy mystery under 300 pages with a high rating, not too old.
note: Single Recommend with semantic_input (cozy mystery) plus max_pages, min_rating, min_year. Four constraints wrapped in one natural sentence.

query: Compare Moby Dick, Don Quixote, and War and Peace on length and writing style.
note: Three FindByTitle then Compare with comparison_criteria. First three-book compare — depends_on must list all three retrieval nodes.

query: Recommend me books like Sapiens and The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck — non-fiction, high rated, under 400 pages, after 2010.
note: Two FindByTitle then Recommend with genre + min_rating + max_pages + min_year filters. Complex filter set on a two-reference recommendation.

query: Recommend me books like The Name of the Wind, but exclude anything by Patrick Rothfuss.
note: FindByTitle then Recommend with an exclusion filter on author. Tests the ExclusionBookFilter path inside BooksFilter.

query: Find me the top 5 most popular children's books with over 1000 ratings.
note: TWO BOUNDS AND A FLAG (re-baselined 2026-08-20): is_children plus min_ratings_count, no subject. 'Top 5' is a count this node cannot express — it reports how many matched and previews a few, which is the accepted cost of superlatives-as-bounds. Previously expected Retrieve_Popular.

query: What should I read after finishing The Lord of the Rings trilogy?
note: FindByTitle then Recommend. Phrasing is about 'after finishing a series' — LLM must map this to a reference-based recommendation.

query: Compare 1984 and Brave New World, then recommend something similar to whichever feels darker.
note: Two FindByTitle + Compare + Recommend. Four-node chain where Recommend depends on the Compare output — tests deep dependency chain.

query: Who is the developer? Also, are there any books about the technologies they used to build this app?
note: DeveloperInfo + ProjectInfo + FindByTraits/Recommend across three domains. The tech stack from ProjectInfo informs the book search — cross-domain dependency.

query: I want fantasy books similar to both Lord of the Rings and A Song of Ice and Fire — highly rated, after 2005, not too long.
note: Two FindByTitle then Recommend with multiple filters. Tricky because 'not too long' requires LLM inference for max_pages from context of epic fantasy.

query: I want something completely different — no sci-fi, no fantasy, no romance. Something literary, thought-provoking, 300-500 pages, highly rated, post-2000, and nothing by Cormac McCarthy.
note: Single Recommend with complex semantic_input, page range, min_rating, min_year, and multi-field exclusion (categories + author). Tests negative constraint handling.

query: Compare Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone and The Lion the Witch and the Wardrobe in terms of their magic systems and coming-of-age themes.
note: Two FindByTitle + Compare with rich comparison_criteria. The criteria span two distinct dimensions — tests multi-criteria extraction into a single field.

query: Who is the developer and what is their email? Also, I'd like to send them some feedback: the recommendation quality is excellent but it could be faster.
note: DeveloperInfo + Feedback across two domains in one message. Tests dual-node resolution with contact_info from DeveloperInfo surfacing next to a Feedback node.

query: Find me books like Dune but also like The Lord of the Rings — something epic, philosophically deep, highly rated, over 500 pages, fiction, published after 1980, and please exclude George R.R. Martin.
note: Two FindByTitle + Recommend with semantic_input, genre, min_pages, min_rating, min_year, and author exclusion. Six simultaneous constraints on a two-reference recommendation.

query: Compare The Alchemist and The Little Prince on themes, then recommend a modern novel that blends both their themes but is grounded in realism.
note: Two FindByTitle + Compare + Recommend. The Recommend semantic_input must synthesize the comparison result — four-node chain with semantic chaining between Compare and Recommend.

query: Compare the writing styles of The Old Man and the Sea, The Great Gatsby, and The Sound and the Fury, then recommend a modern novel (post-2000) that echoes the most impactful one, under 400 pages.
note: Three FindByTitle + Compare + Recommend. Five nodes with criteria-focused compare and filtered recommendation — tests maximum Compare fan-in before Recommend.

query: Hello! What's your name? Also tell me about this project and recommend me a sci-fi book.
note: Small talk + ProjectInfo + Recommend. Tests that the planner correctly separates small_talk from two real goals without over-routing.

query: Compare Harry Potter, Narnia, A Wizard of Earthsea, and The Magicians in terms of their magic systems — then recommend something that captures the best of all four.
note: Four FindByTitle + Compare + Recommend. Six-node chain — the largest legal fan-in for Compare; tests that all four depends_on ids are resolved before Compare runs.

query: I'm a developer who uses this app. Show me my token usage, tell me about the project's tech stack, and recommend sci-fi books about distributed systems.
note: UserInfo + ProjectInfo + Recommend across all three domains simultaneously. Three parallel nodes before Recommend — tests multi-domain fan-in.

query: I want to explore dystopian fiction. Compare 1984, Brave New World, and Fahrenheit 451 on their visions of government control, then recommend 3 modern novels (post-2010) from non-Western perspectives that continue this tradition — highly rated and not too long.
note: Three FindByTitle + Compare + Recommend. Five nodes with thematic comparison_criteria, geographic semantic modifier, multiple filters, and implicit limit=3. Tests the full complexity of the planner pipeline.

query: Can you look up my previous conversations, then based on any books I mentioned, recommend something I haven't read yet?
note: UserInfo(previous_conversation) + Recommend. The Recommend depends on UserInfo output — cross-domain sequential dependency where book data is derived from user history, not a static reference.

query: Compare Dune, Foundation, and Neuromancer on world-building and technology themes. Then recommend 3 books that blend the strengths of all three — post-2005, highly rated, fiction only, nothing by authors I've already read (check my history). Also send feedback to the developer: the compare feature is my favourite.
note: Three FindByTitle + Compare + UserInfo + Recommend + Feedback. Seven nodes across book and user domains. The Recommend exclusion depends on UserInfo output; Feedback runs in parallel. Maximum realistic complexity for this system.

query: Did Jane Austen write Dune?
note: Authorship verification (design-intent expectation, updated 2026-07-28 when FindByTitle lost its authors hint field). Now the same shape as case 7: Retrieve_by_Title + Retrieve_by_Author + Combine_Intersect, where the empty intersection IS the 'no' — the question is answered against the data rather than by an unvalidated hint. The failure to catch is reading 'Jane Austen' as a bibliography search and returning her catalogue.

query: What books has Ursula K. Le Guin written?
note: Single FindByAuthor. The plain one-author bibliography — the baseline case the node exists for, and the control for the multi-author cases below.

query: Show me books by Jane Austen and books by Paulo Coelho.
note: Two separate bibliographies → one FindByAuthor per author, mirroring FindByTitle's one-node-per-title rule. The failure to catch is collapsing both names into a single node, which the old authors: list[str] schema allowed and the single-author split removed.

query: What did Brian Herbert and Kevin J. Anderson write together?
note: Single FindByCoAuthors. 'together' is the collaboration signal: both names belong on ONE node as an AND, not two separate bibliographies. The mirror image of case 53 — same two-name shape, opposite plan — so the pair is what actually tests whether the planner reads the collaboration cue instead of just counting names.

query: Did Neil Gaiman and Terry Pratchett ever co-write anything?
note: Single FindByCoAuthors, phrased as a yes/no. An empty result is the real answer to this one, so it checks the planner routes the question to the node rather than refusing it or fabricating a bibliography.

query: Show me fantasy books by Brandon Sanderson.
note: MULTI-ANCHOR CONTROL (re-baselined 2026-08-24; expected Retrieve_by_Author alone from 2026-07-24). Two anchor dimensions in one request: author AND genre. The original expectation picked the more selective anchor and dropped the genre, because no combine node was registered and emitting both as siblings would UNION them. Combine_Intersect makes the intersection expressible, so the honest plan is both retrievals plus the intersect. Case 65's note had been asking for this re-decision since the combine tier was designed. Genre is near-redundant here (Sanderson writes almost only fantasy), which is exactly what makes 56 the control and 57 the test.

query: What children's books has Neil Gaiman written?
note: MULTI-ANCHOR, LOAD-BEARING GENRE (re-baselined 2026-08-24 alongside 56). Same shape as case 56, opposite stakes: Gaiman writes across adult and children's fiction, so dropping the genre returns a materially wrong bibliography rather than a slightly wide one. That is why the old pick-one-anchor expectation was always a compromise, and why this pair is the argument the combine tier settles. The audience half rides on the lexical node (audience=children), so the goals report still compares node TYPES only and cannot see whether it was captured — this case remains the argument for argument-level checking.

query: Find books between 300 and 500 pages published after 2015.
note: ANCHORLESS CONSTRAINTS (was a design-intent no-node expectation, 2026-07-24; re-baselined 2026-08-20). The premise changed rather than the plan being fixed: page count and year can now BE what a search is about, via Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits. Mirrors case 12.

query: Show me romance books by Nora Roberts and mystery books by Agatha Christie.
note: MULTI-ANCHOR x2 (re-baselined 2026-08-24 alongside 56/57). Two authors, each with their own genre, and the two halves are ALTERNATIVES rather than one intersection — so it is two independent intersections, not one over all four retrievals. That is the distinction Combine_Intersect's `Do not use:` states: "romance by Roberts and mystery by Christie" is two answers, not one. The failure to catch is collapsing it into a single intersect, which asks for books that are romance AND mystery AND by Roberts AND by Christie, and correctly returns nothing.

query: Find me some books by Jane Austen and Neil Gaiman with 200 pages or more, in thriller, before 2020. And recommend me some books like them with rating 4.0+ and at least 1000 ratings.
note: CONSTRAINT-DENSE TWO-STAGE (design-intent expectation, added 2026-07-24). The heaviest case in the suite: two authors and five constraints split across two stages. Stage 1 is case 53's shape (two separate bibliographies, one Retrieve_by_Author each) with three constraints hung on each node — pages >= 200, thriller, before 2020 — none of which is an anchor. Stage 2 is 'like them' plus two more constraints (rating >= 4.0, ratings_count >= 1000), which is Analyze_Similar_Books depending on both retrievals. So three nodes, not five: no Retrieve_by_Lexical_Traits for thriller, no separate node for the page or year filters. Two distinct failures to catch: (a) promoting a constraint to an anchor node, which unions instead of narrowing, and (b) losing the dependency link so the recommendation runs off the raw query rather than the retrieved books. Also a live example of the argument-level blind spot — the goals report can confirm the three node types and still miss every one of the five constraints.

query: Show me Haruki Murakami books published after 2005.
note: RETRIEVAL CONSTRAINT (re-baselined 2026-08-24; previously Retrieve_by_Author + Filter_Retrieval). A known subject narrowed by a metadata bound, with no similarity ask anywhere in the query. The year bound is now its own retrieval (min_year=2006 on Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits) and the intersect is what makes it narrow rather than widen. Two failures to catch: routing to Analyze_Similar_Books because a metadata bound appeared (nothing here asks for anything *like* anything), and emitting the two retrievals without the intersect, which pools them.

query: Recommend me something like Neuromancer but under 300 pages.
note: RECOMMENDATION CONSTRAINT (added 2026-07-24, re-baselined 2026-08-24 — the premise reversed twice). It expected Retrieve_by_Title + Analyze_Similar_Books alone, with the bound left in the similarity goal's description for that node's own parse to route into its vector search's WHERE. Both halves of that are now gone: Analyze_Similar_Books stopped parsing anything (2026-08-22), and the argument it rested on — that filtering a ranked pool afterwards throws the ranking away — was a property of materialized ROWS, not of a scored deferred query. Combine_Intersect carries the pool's cosine score through the narrowing (compose(op="and")), so the bound is its own retrieval and the ranking survives. The count then means "of the 250 nearest, N are also under 300 pages". The failure to catch is now the old expectation: dropping the bound entirely because the similarity node has nowhere to put it.

query: Show me Octavia Butler books over 300 pages, and recommend similar books rated 4.0 or higher.
note: PARTIALLY UNSATISFIABLE — FLAGGED, NOT CLEANLY RE-BASELINED (2026-08-24). The first half is an ordinary bounded bibliography: Retrieve_by_Author + Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits (min_pages=300) + Combine_Intersect. The second half ("recommend similar books rated 4.0 or higher") CANNOT be planned as written: Analyze_Similar_Books requires list[BookAnchorOutput], Retrieve_by_Author returns a candidate, and Combine_Intersect's output lands on the base — so nothing in this plan can anchor a similarity search. That is the deliberate cost of the 2026-08-22 anchors/candidates split ("books like Frank Herbert's" is a semantic ask, not an anchored one), not a regression this change introduced. The expectation covers only the half the taxonomy can serve; it needs re-deciding together with whether an author bibliography should ever be anchorable.

query: Recommend books like The Road, then only keep the ones with at least 1000 ratings.
note: POST-FILTER PHRASING TRAP (added 2026-07-24, re-baselined 2026-08-24). The wording explicitly describes a post-filter — recommend first, THEN keep some — and the correct plan used to ignore it, because filtering a ranked list after the fact threw the ranking away. It no longer does: Combine_Intersect narrows the similarity pool in SQL and compose(op="and") carries the cosine score through, so the literal reading is now the right one and the trap is defused rather than tested. What is still worth catching is the bound going nowhere — Analyze_Similar_Books parses nothing since 2026-08-22, so 'at least 1000 ratings' has no home except its own Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits goal. Kept as a live case for that, not for the syntax-vs-semantics question it was written for.

query: What horror books has Stephen King written that are over 500 pages?
note: FULL COMBINE TIER (re-baselined 2026-08-24; was four nodes ending in Filter_Retrieval). Still the longest correct plan in the suite, but a different shape: three retrievals feeding ONE intersect, because Combine_Intersect is n-ary where Filter_Retrieval was single-input. The line this case used to draw — "horror is a search subject and gets a retrieval node, 500 pages is a constraint and cannot" — was the numbers-only rule, and it is retired: a bound is a retrieval like any other. Two failures to catch: emitting the retrievals as bare siblings, which pools them (every King book OR every horror book OR every long book) instead of intersecting; and chaining two intersects where one with three dependencies is correct. COLLISION WITH 56/57/59 RESOLVED — those were re-baselined to the same shape the same day.

query: Recommend me a book.
note: BARE RECOMMEND (design-intent expectation, added 2026-07-28 with Retrieve_Random's promotion to V1 core). The word 'recommend' is present but no taste is: no anchor title, no mood, no genre. Analyze_Similar_Books needs a supporting retrieval and there is nothing to build one from, so the honest plan is a single Retrieve_Random and nothing after it — the node already returns a book, so there is nothing for an analyze step to rank. Tests whether the planner routes on the verb or on whether the user actually expressed a preference. Two failures to catch: Analyze_Similar_Books over an invented anchor, and Retrieve_Random + Analyze_Similar_Books.

query: Surprise me with a book, but keep it under 200 pages and well rated.
note: BOUNDED SURPRISE (design-intent expectation, added 2026-07-28; note updated 2026-08-24). 'Surprise me' cedes the choice, so this is Retrieve_Random, and both bounds go in its own filters where the pick is drawn from inside them. No combine node may be emitted: intersecting a single arbitrary pick against anything discards it far more often than not, answering with nothing that looks identical to 'no matches'. The ban was Filter_Retrieval's until that node was replaced; it transferred to Combine_Intersect unchanged, and both docstrings state it. The failure to catch is Retrieve_Random + Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits + Combine_Intersect.

query: Recommend me a J.K. Rowling book.
note: AUTHOR-ANCHORED RECOMMEND (design-intent expectation, added 2026-07-28). The author-shaped twin of case 3 ('recommend me a mystery book' → Retrieve_by_Lexical_Traits + Analyze_Similar_Books); the suite had title anchors (16, 20, 22) and genre anchors (3, 11) but no author anchor, so this fills the last corner of the recommend triangle. The author is the taste signal: retrieve her catalog, then pick from it. TWO failures to catch, one on each side. (a) Retrieve_by_Author alone, which answers case 52's question instead — the user asked for ONE book chosen for them, not the bibliography. (b) Retrieve_Random: this query is case 66's 'Recommend me a book' with four words inserted, and 'recommend me a book' is a literal Example query in Retrieve_Random's docstring, so 66 and 68 together are the actual test of whether the planner reads the anchor or pattern-matches the phrasing. The named author is exactly the 'taste, mood or anchor' that Retrieve_Random's Do-not-use clause routes away.

query: Compare Dune and IT on writing style, then recommend something based on the scarier one.
note: COMPARE ON ONE AXIS, PIVOT ON ANOTHER (added 2026-07-28). Node-wise this is case 36 again — two Retrieve_by_Title, Analyze_Compare, Analyze_Similar_Books — and it is here for what happens INSIDE the nodes, which the goals report cannot see. The compare is explicitly scoped ('on writing style') while the pivot that selects the anchor is a different attribute ('the scarier one'), so the two criteria words must land in different nodes: 'writing style' in Analyze_Compare.comparison_criteria, 'scarier' in Analyze_Similar_Books.semantic_input. Three failures to catch, only the first of which the node diff sees: dropping the recommend and answering with the comparison alone (the phrasing 'recommend on the scarier one' can be misread as 'tell me which one to read'); folding 'scarier' into comparison_criteria, which produces a report on the right books along the wrong axis; and pointing Analyze_Similar_Books at the two title retrievals instead of at the compare, which quietly recommends from BOTH books pooled rather than from whichever the report picked. Worth noting the design tension it exposes: a report scoped to writing style does not actually contain the scariness verdict the pivot needs.

query: Recommend 2 books like Dune and compare them.
note: COMPARE OVER A RECOMMENDATION (design-intent expectation, added 2026-07-28). The first case where Analyze_Compare's input is not named books but books the system just chose: Retrieve_by_Title(Dune) → Analyze_Similar_Books → Analyze_Compare depending on the recommend node. Every other compare case (17, 23, 31, 36, 40, 43, 44, 46, 48) hangs the compare off one retrieval per named title, so this is the only test of the BookRecommendationOutput → Analyze_Compare edge that the shape vocabulary declares legal. KNOWN CONTRADICTION with the current docstrings, which is the point of the case: Analyze_Compare says 'depends_on: at least 2 nodes that produce books' and 'Use when: the user wants a side-by-side read on specific named books', but the correct plan here has exactly ONE upstream node carrying two books and no named titles. The arity that matters for a comparison is two BOOKS, not two nodes; the wording has not been fixed yet, so expect this red until it is. Second, unrelated gap it exposes: Analyze_Similar_Books has no limit field, so the '2' is unexpressible and will be silently dropped whatever the planner emits. The failure to catch is a second Retrieve_by_Title (or a fabricated one for an invented comparison partner) to satisfy the two-node reading.

query: Find the Dune books that are over 500 pages.
note: TITLE + BOUND (added 2026-08-17, re-baselined 2026-08-24). Case 61's shape drawn on a title anchor. Every node in this plan is registered and has an executor, which makes it the case that exercises the intersect executor and the composed-query hand-off end to end rather than routing alone. Two failures to catch: folding the page bound into Retrieve_by_Title, which carries no filters and would drop it; and omitting the intersect, which pools the title match with every long book in the catalog.

query: Show me some well rated books.
note: INFERRED BOUND, NO FIGURE (added 2026-08-20). 'Well rated' has to become min_rating 4.0 from the calibration on BookMetadataFilter's field descriptions — this is the core of what Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits adds over a literal numeric filter, and it is why the slice has its own parser prompt: the shared basic_fill_schema_prompt says 'do not use prior knowledge', which returns an empty filter here.

query: What books do you have from the classical period?
note: INFERRED YEAR BOUND (added 2026-08-20): 'classical period' -> max_year 1970. Regression guard — an earlier field description that opened with the corpus range made the parser answer 1876, the oldest book in the catalog, rather than the calibrated cutoff.

query: Find me obscure books nobody has heard of.
note: RATINGS COUNT, NOT RATING (added 2026-08-20). 'Obscure' is max_ratings_count 1000 and says nothing about quality; the two rating columns are the pair most easily swapped. This case stayed empty under the shared no-inference parser prompt and at reasoning_effort=minimal.

query: I want something really long.
note: INFERRED PAGE BOUND (added 2026-08-20): 'really long' -> min_pages 500. At reasoning_effort=minimal the parser invented min_pages 1000 instead of using the calibrated value, so this pins the calibration being read rather than a plausible number being guessed.

query: Find me books over 400 pages.
note: POSITIVE HALF of the discrimination pair with case 77 (added 2026-08-20, note updated 2026-08-24). No other subject, so the bound IS the search and one node is the whole plan. What the pair tests changed with the numbers-only rule's retirement: both halves now use Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits, and the discriminator is whether a second condition — and therefore Combine_Intersect — is present. The failure to catch is emitting a combine node over a single retrieval, which the input contract refuses for needing 2+ dependencies.

query: Find me fantasy books over 400 pages.
note: PAIR WITH CASE 76 (added 2026-08-20, re-baselined 2026-08-24). Same bound, one added subject. This pair used to hold the numbers-only rule — 76 routes to Retrieve_by_Numeric_Traits alone, 77 must NOT. That rule is retired: 77 now uses the numeric node TOO, and what the pair holds instead is the intersect. 76 has one condition and takes no combine node; 77 has two and requires one. The failure to catch is emitting both retrievals for 77 and stopping there, which pools them and answers with every fantasy book plus every long book.

query: Recommend books like Dune and explain why each one fits.
note: EXPLICIT EXPLANATION. The plan is identical to case 16's — the explanation is not a separate capability and not a goal at all, since the reply is written after every goal has run (deregistered 2026-09-08). The failure to catch is a second goal for "explain", or an Analyze_Compare over the pool: nothing compares here, the reply writer justifies the picks from the anchor and the searched-for description on its own.

query: Do you have The Silmarillion? If so recommend something like it, and tell me why.
note: ONE CHAIN, ONE REPLY (added 2026-09-07). A chained ask — the lookup is the anchor for the similarity search, not a separate answer — so it is ONE generation goal at the end, not one per part. This is also the case that exercises the failure path end to end when the title misses: the retrieval finds nothing, the similarity goal is skipped, and the generation goal still runs, reading the failure artifact so the reply can say why there is nothing to show.
